paras: The threatened lynching of Will Johnson was a mob threat in August 1890 against a Black boy, also named as John or Joe Johnson, held in the jail at Opelika, Alabama, after he was accused of burglary, of wounding several men and of killing Jenkins Moore, a merchant and justice of the peace at Gold Hill. A mob threatened the jail but made no attack after the sheriff placed a guard around it. Papers across the country carried the story, stressing the boy's reported age of fourteen and casting him as a "desperado."

According to a Montgomery dispatch of August 7 that cited a special to the Advertiser, Will Johnson, "a negro boy," burglarized two houses in Opelika on August 6 and the next day killed P. J. Moore, a Gold Hill merchant who was trying to arrest him. A fuller Birmingham dispatch printed in the New York Sun gave his name as John Johnson and his age as fourteen, and said he was caught robbing the house of a Mrs. McClellan in Opelika. Another Birmingham report called him Joe Johnson and said he entered Mrs. McClellan's house "for the double purpose of assaulting and burglarizing," adding a charge of assaulting "a respectable white woman."

In the Sun's account, a young white man named Green tried to capture the boy and was slightly wounded, after which Johnson hid in an empty box car and shot a watchman named Ingram in the breast. A man named Stringfellow then chased and overtook him and was shot in the head, a wound described as probably fatal. Johnson reached Gold Hill, seven miles away, where officers had telegraphed his description ahead, and Moore, described as a justice of the peace and the town's leading merchant, tried to arrest him and was shot through the heart. A crowd, "crowds of white men" in the Washington Evening Star's version, pursued him; he fired several shots without hitting anyone and was run down and captured once his cartridges were spent. The Indianapolis Journal placed the Stringfellow shooting at Gold Hill instead, saying that Stringfellow, a track-walker who had seen Moore killed, grabbed the boy and was shot through the forehead in the scuffle.

Johnson was taken back to Opelika and jailed. The Sun reported that he had confessed to killing a white man some time earlier and to having "started out to be a train robber and desperado." That night a mob threatened the jail but, in the Sun's words, "was overawed by the guard provided by the Sheriff." The Evening Star said a mob "was organized to lynch the boy" but made no attack because of the strong guard. A Birmingham dispatch of August 9 said Sheriff McGraw had set the guard after hearing that a lynching would be attempted, and that "a large crowd" stood outside the jail "intent upon lynching the prisoner."

No report of Johnson's fate after August 10, whether he was tried, harmed or moved, appears in the coverage. On August 16 the Huntsville Gazette reported only that John Johnson, fourteen, had been arrested at Opelika, where he was "wanted for a dozen crimes," including murder, highway robbery, burglary and grand larceny. That brief said the boy had been a fugitive for some time and was captured while robbing a private residence, and it did not mention a mob.

All the coverage found appeared in white daily and weekly papers between August 8 and August 16, and no Black-press report was found. The first wire, from Montgomery, ran on August 8 in the Richmond Dispatch, the Savannah Morning News, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Pittsburg Dispatch, under headlines such as "Negro Burglar and Murderer," "Ready For a Lynching" and "May Be Strung Up." A shorter version saying Johnson "was captured, and there are threats of lynching" appeared in the Wilmington Evening Journal and the Clarksville Daily Tobacco Leaf-Chronicle, and the Montgomery text was still being reprinted in the Manning Times and the Hillsboro News-Herald a week later.

The Birmingham account ran in the Sun under "Started Out to Be a Desperado," and the Washington Evening Star printed it as "Precocious and Depraved," calling the boy "a Burglar and Murderer at Fourteen." Western papers reprinted that account through mid-August under headlines including "A Youthful Desperado," "A Boy's Awful Crimes" and "An Alabama Negro Kills Several White Men." The Deseret Evening News and the Indianapolis Journal carried the version with the assault charge, the Journal under a headline describing "An Alabama Negro Who Has Shot Six People and Killed Three of Them," a count that included two earlier killings of white men its text attributed to him. Across these versions the shootings and the confession were stated as fact, and the lynching threats were reported without comment.

Reports differed on the boy's name: Will Johnson in the Montgomery wire, John Johnson in the Sun, the Evening Star and the Huntsville Gazette, and Joe Johnson in the Deseret Evening News and the Indianapolis Journal. They also differed on Moore's name, given as P. J. Moore in the Montgomery wire and Jenkins Moore in the Birmingham reports, and on the number of people shot, four in the Deseret Evening News and six in the Indianapolis Journal's headline. The timing varied as well: the Montgomery wire placed Moore's killing on August 7, while the Indianapolis Journal's August 9 dispatch said it happened "Yesterday afternoon." Only the Deseret and Indianapolis versions charged an assault on a woman; the Sun and the Evening Star described a robbery.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Will Johnson
bases: A mob organized to lynch a Black boy held in the Opelika jail but was kept off by the sheriff's guard (A6, A7, A10), a threatened lynching.
A mob gathered to lynch Johnson for the shootings he was accused of, which meets the group and pretext parts (A6, A7, A10), but no report says he was killed; the mob 'made no attack' (A7).

Three independent dispatches, the Montgomery wire (A1), the Birmingham account in the Sun (A6) and a separate Birmingham account (A8, A10), agree on the shootings charged to Johnson, his capture and jailing, and the lynching threats.

accounts.label: Montgomery wire (Advertiser special)
accounts.gist: Will Johnson burglarized two Opelika houses on Aug 6 and on Aug 7 killed P. J. Moore of Gold Hill, who was trying to arrest him; lynching threats were made.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire (Sun version)
accounts.gist: John Johnson, 14, caught robbing Mrs. McClellan's house, shot Green, Ingram and Stringfellow while fleeing, then killed Jenkins Moore at Gold Hill; a crowd captured him; a mob threatened the jail but was overawed by the sheriff's guard.

accounts.label: Birmingham wire (Indianapolis Journal version)
accounts.gist: Joe Johnson entered Mrs. McClellan's house to assault and burglarize; Stringfellow was shot at Gold Hill after grabbing him; Sheriff McGraw guarded the jail as a large crowd gathered intent on lynching.

accounts.label: Huntsville Gazette brief
accounts.gist: John Johnson, 14, was arrested at Opelika, wanted for a dozen crimes, and captured while robbing a private residence; no mob is mentioned.

framing.detail: The Montgomery wire ran under 'Negro Burglar and Murderer', 'Ready For a Lynching' and 'May Be Strung Up', forecasting a lynching without comment.

The Sun ('Started Out to Be a Desperado') and the Evening Star ('Precocious and Depraved') told the story as a boy's crime spree, printing the alleged confession as fact and noting the guard that stopped the mob.
Western reprints headlined 'A Youthful Desperado' and 'An Alabama Negro Kills Several White Men'.
The Indianapolis Journal and Deseret versions added an alleged assault on 'a respectable white woman' and earlier killings of white men.

conflicts.note: The two Birmingham accounts and the Montgomery wire each give a different first name; none is clearly better evidence.
